issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette:
Hector has spent forty years mastering the language of the body, but now, at sixty-two, he finds himself unable to speak about the one event that has come to define him. Six months ago, his car was T-boned at an intersection. He remembers the afternoon light glinting off the storefronts and a brief, foolish moment of vanity as he caught his own reflection, admiring the posture he still held even when driving. Then came the sound—a high-pitched, metallic scream that seemed to tear the air apart, followed by a deafening, percussive crunch. The memory exists for him not as a narrative, but as a sensory assault. When his wife, Sofia, asks him to describe it, the words catch in his throat; he can only shake his head, gesturing vaguely, the story trapped somewhere behind his eyes. He cannot seem to put the frightening event into words. The sound, however, needs no invitation. It plays in his head when a truck screeches its brakes outside their apartment, or a dish shatters in the kitchen, a perfect auditory recreation of the impact. With the sound comes a wave of hot, suffocating shame. He is certain the crash happened because of that moment of pride, a punishment for the vanity of an aging dancer. The event happened to him, he has come to believe, because of the sort of person he is.

In the weeks that followed the collision, Hector’s world began to shrink. The dance studio, once his sanctuary, became a landscape of perceived threats. Before rehearsal, while others stretched, he would find himself compulsively scanning the room, mapping the path to the fire escape, his heart pounding until he had a viable exit strategy. His body, once an instrument of grace, became a source of alarm. During a partner lift, another dancer’s hand on his back made him flinch so violently he nearly dropped her. He saw the shock in her eyes and felt that familiar, sickening shame. He has come to live in a state of constant, low-grade dread, a world drained of its former colour. He watches Sofia laugh at a joke on television and feels a profound and terrifying distance, a gray numbness where joy used to be. He is convinced he will never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the crash broke something essential inside him. This sense of immutable damage feeds a deeper fear: that he is utterly powerless, a passenger in a life where terrible things can happen at any moment, without reason or warning.

To manage this internal chaos, Hector has developed a rigid set of defenses. He fights an hourly battle against his own mind, actively trying to push away any thought of the accident. When a fragment of memory surfaces—the sound, the feeling of spinning—he shoves it down with brute mental force. The nights are the worst. He waits until Sofia is breathing deeply beside him and then slips out of bed, staying up until dawn watching old black-and-white films, deliberately exhausting himself to keep the nightmares at bay. His most practiced escape, however, is one that feels like a betrayal of his life’s work. When a trigger is unavoidable—a sudden loud noise, an unexpected touch—he has taught himself to deliberately leave his body. He fixes his gaze on a neutral point and mentally floats away, blanking out the world. The strategy offers a moment of relief, but it is costing him his career. During a recent rehearsal, a car horn blared from the street and Hector checked out. He missed his cue entirely, his body still on the floor when it should have been in the air, causing a chain reaction that nearly injured a colleague. It was after this incident, seeing the mix of fear and frustration on the faces of his troupe, that Sofia insisted he seek help. Hector now sits in the therapist’s office, terrified of what dredging up the past will do, but more terrified of the life he is currently living: a silent, grayed-out existence in a body he no longer recognizes as his own.
